## What are Stochastic Games?

Stochastic games (Shapley, 1953) are multi-player dynamic games
in which a finite set of agents interact repeatedly over time in a shared,
evolving environment. At each stage, every player observes the current
**state** of the system, simultaneously chooses an **action**, receives a
**payoff**, and the system transitions to a new state according to a Markov
kernel that depends on the joint action profile. Each player aims to optimize
their cumulative (discounted or average) payoff over the horizon.

Stochastic games unify and generalize two classical frameworks: **Markov
Decision Processes** (MDPs) (the single-agent special case) and **repeated games**
(the special case where the state never changes). The central solution concept
is the **Markov Perfect Equilibrium (MPE)** - a profile of state-dependent
strategies, one per player, such that no player can gain by deviating, given
the others' strategies.

## Formal model

:::{.definition data-title="Markov decision process (one player)"}

An MDP is a tuple $\Gamma=(S,A,N_{T},\mu_{0},P,r)$ where $S$ is a finite state
set; $A(s)$ is the finite set of actions available in state $s$; $N_{T}>0$ is
the number of time steps with time set $\mathcal{T}=\{0,1,\dots,N_{T}\}$;
$\mu_{0}\in\mathcal{P}(S)$ is the initial state distribution (here
$\mathcal{P}(X)$ is the set of probability distributions on $X$);
$P_{n}(s,a)\in\mathcal{P}(S)$ is the law of the next state given action $a$ in
state $s$ at time $n$; and $r_{n}(s,a)\in\mathbb{R}$ is the payoff of action
$a$ in state $s$ at time $n$.

:::

A **policy** is a map $\pi:\mathcal{T}\times S\to\mathcal{P}(A)$ giving the
distribution of actions in each state at each time; it is **pure** when this
distribution is a Dirac mass. The agent maximizes the cumulative expected
reward
$$
J(\pi)=\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{n=0}^{N_{T}}r_{n}(s_{n},a_{n})\right],\qquad
a_{n}\sim\pi_{n}(s_{n}),\ s_{n+1}\sim P_{n}(s_{n},a_{n}),\ s_{0}\sim\mu_{0}.
$$
This is the discrete-time setting of [[stochastic-control]].

:::{.definition data-title="Discrete-time N-player stochastic game"}

An $N$-player game is a tuple
$(\vec{S},\vec{A},N_{T},\vec{\mu}_{0},\vec{P},\vec{r})$ with state sets
$\vec{S}=(S^{i})_{i\le N}$, action sets $A^{i}(s^{i})$, initial distributions
$\mu_{0}^{i}$, transition rules $P^{i}_{n}$ giving the next state of player $i$
as a function of the current joint state and joint action, and payoffs
$r^{i}_{n}$ for each player $i$. Each player chooses a policy $\pi^{i}$ to
maximize her own expected cumulative payoff given the policies of the others,
and the solution concept is a [[nash-equilibrium|Nash equilibrium]] in policies.

:::

In continuous time the agent chooses a square-integrable control process
$\alpha=(\alpha_{t})_{t\in[0,T]}$ with values in a closed, convex, bounded set
$A\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{k}$, to minimize an expected cost over $[0,T]$ (or an
infinite horizon). See [[control-theory]] and [[mean-field-games]].

## Topics in Stochastic Games

- ***Preliminaries***
	- [[stochastic-processes]]
		- Markov Processes
		- Martingales
	- [[stochastic-differential-equations]]
	- [[stochastic-control]]
- ***Foundations***
	- Formal model: states, action spaces, transition kernel, stage payoffs,
   horizon
	- Relationship to MDPs and repeated games
	- Equilibrium concepts: Nash, Sub-game Perfect, Markov Perfect, Correlated
	- Existence results (Shapley 1953, Fink 1964)
	- Computational complexity (PPAD-hardness of general-sum MPE)
- ***Discrete-Time Stochastic Games***
	- Finite-horizon games and backward induction
	- Infinite-horizon discounted payoff
	- Infinite-horizon average (ergodic) payoff
	- Zero-sum games
		- Shapley operator and value iteration
		- Policy / strategy iteration (Hoffman-Karp)
		- Linear programming formulation
	- General-sum N-player games
		- Nash value iteration and convergence conditions
		- Homotopy / continuation methods (Herings-Peeters)
		- Nonlinear complementarity and mathematical programming formulations
		- Correlated equilibrium and no-regret learning
- ***Continuous-Time Stochastic Games***
	- Differential games (deterministic dynamics)
	- Stochastic differential games (SDE-driven state)
	- Zero-sum differential games and the Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equation
	- Non-zero-sum differential games and coupled HJB systems
- ***Special Structural Classes***
	- Potential games and Markov potential games
	- Super-modular / monotone stochastic games
	- Symmetric and anonymous games
	- Cooperative stochastic games and the core
- ***[[mean-field-games]]***
	- Finite-N to mean-field limit (propagation of chaos)
	- Discrete-time mean-field games
	- Continuous-time mean-field games
		- HJB + [[fokker-planck-equation]] system
		- McKean-Vlasov control
		- Linear-quadratic mean-field games
	- Mean-field games with major and minor players
	- Numerical methods for mean-field games
- Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
	- Nash-Q learning
	- Policy gradient and actor-critic methods
	- Two-timescale stochastic approximation
	- No-regret dynamics and convergence to equilibrium
	- MARL in the mean-field regime
- Heterogeneous Agent Games
	- Markov-perfect industry dynamics (Ericson-Pakes framework)
	- Oblivious equilibrium as a scalable approximation
	- Computational methods for heterogeneous-state MPE
- Applications
	- Dynamic industrial organization and oligopoly
	- Finance: optimal stopping, systemic risk, algorithmic trading
	- Robotics and autonomous multi-agent systems
	- Evolutionary biology and population games

## References

- A. Neyman and S. Sorin (eds.), *Stochastic Games and Applications*.
